brief: Verdict ahead of the print: few doubt that Alphabet beats the quarter. The shares will move on four things: how fast Google Cloud grows (the Street is near 90% against 82% in 2Q26), whether Cloud margins hold now that rented third-party capacity is coming in, the first 2027 capex framework (Street talk runs from about $300bn to about $330bn), and how management funds a free cash flow line that has gone negative. Alphabet confirmed on 6 October 2026 that it reports on Wednesday 28 October 2026 after the close, with the call at 4:30 pm ET.

Where expectations sit. Yahoo Finance shows 3Q26 revenue consensus of $127.85bn from 41 analysts (range $123.41bn to $138.68bn), up 24.9% on $102.35bn, and EPS of $3.00 from 44 analysts (range $2.25 to $3.63) against $2.87 a year ago. MarketBeat has $127.92bn and $2.96, and Drillr's survey has $3.04. Zacks puts Google Cloud revenue at $29.16bn, up 92.4% on $15.16bn. BofA reports the Street at 89% Cloud growth against its own 93%. Zacks' total revenue of $111.64bn and BofA's Street figure of $111.0bn appear to be net of TAC; this is our inference, since $127.85bn less Zacks' $16.53bn of TAC gives $111.32bn. Neither source states the basis. We found no published consensus for Cloud operating income, backlog or quarterly capex.

What the last call set up. In July, CFO Anat Ashkenazi raised 2026 capex guidance to $195bn to $205bn (from $180bn to $190bn, and $175bn to $185bn in February), and said capex will 'increase significantly in 2027'. H1 capex was $80.6bn, so the guide implies $57bn to $62bn a quarter in the second half. She also guided to 'modest margin pressure' in Cloud as Google expands third-party capacity in 3Q as a 'bridging strategy', and said free cash flow 'will remain under pressure'. 2Q26 free cash flow was -$5.9bn. Cloud backlog was $514bn, up more than $50bn in the quarter, with just over half to be recognized within 24 months. TPU systems sold into customer data centers began to be recognized in 2Q26, with 'the vast majority' of revenue in 2027.

Three debates. First, the capex-to-cash bridge: the Street has FY26 capex at about $202bn (BofA) and FY26 free cash flow of only $7.07bn (S&P Global via StockAnalysis), with FY27 free cash flow consensus negative (about -$37bn per Barchart via Yahoo; about -$32bn per TIKR via Admiral Markets). Second, Cloud margin quality, as the 35.6% margin in 2Q26 absorbs rented capacity, including the SpaceX GPU contract (reported at $920mn a month for 32 months from October 2026), and Pichai's 20 October comment that Cloud is giving up revenue so research gets first claim on compute. Third, the off-balance-sheet build: $85.2bn of data center leases not yet commenced, plus a $5.8bn short-term lease starting in 3Q, $43.8bn of credit-derivative backstops of third-party data center payments (up from $16.9bn at year-end), $7.6bn of energy equipment guarantees, and an agreement for an estimated $24.1bn more.

What would move the stock. Positive: Cloud growth at or above 90% with a margin in the mid-30s, backlog well above $514bn as Anthropic's multi-GW TPU capacity and Meta's TPU rental are booked, TPU revenue quantified, and a 2027 capex frame near $300bn with a credible funding mix. Negative: Cloud below about 85%, a margin dip larger than 'modest', a 2027 capex frame well above $330bn with no free cash flow floor, or a sign of more equity issuance beyond the $40bn ATM, which management said is for employee equity taxes. GOOGL closed at $324.22 on 22 October, down 7.2% from $349.22 on 15 October, and traded at about $323.85 early on 23 October. Implied moves run from 5.07% (Pepperstone) to about 6.4% (EarningsWatcher via OANDA).

Kona read-through. Google is now the market's main tenant-credit provider for third-party AI sites. It backstops neocloud leases (Fluidstack at TeraWulf and Cipher) as credit derivatives worth $43.8bn and is lining up another $24.1bn, while it rents GPUs (SpaceX) and sells TPUs into other people's data centers. A small off-grid site can borrow that credit only by fitting the template: a hyperscaler-approved tenant, a long lease, and power that is ready to energize. The call should show how far down the size curve Google will go.
changes: Capex guide raised twice since February: $175bn to $185bn (February), $180bn to $190bn (April), $195bn to $205bn (July), with 2027 to 'increase significantly'. Some previews (InsiderFinance, Plus500) still quote the stale $175bn to $185bn.

Funding shift in June to August: $49.6bn of net equity (common including a $10.0bn Berkshire Hathaway private placement, plus 6.25% mandatory convertible preferred), a $40.0bn ATM, $20.3bn of 2Q notes, then $25bn of US dollar notes on 10 August, rated Aa2/AA+, at T+33 bps (2028) to T+130 bps (2066). Long-term debt was $98.2bn at 30 June, against $46.5bn at year-end.

Off-balance-sheet AI commitments jumped in 2Q26: credit-derivative backstops of third-party data center payments of $43.8bn (from $16.9bn), leases not yet commenced of $85.2bn, total purchase commitments of $811.0bn, and a $20.0bn milestone-based capital funding commitment to a private company. AI Weekly, citing Bloomberg, links Alphabet's large private holding to Anthropic; the 10-Q does not name it.

New compute and power deals: SpaceX GPU capacity (about 110,000 Nvidia GPUs, $920mn a month, 32 months from October 2026; reported from SpaceX's IPO filing); Anthropic's 3.5 GW of TPU capacity from 2027 (Broadcom filing, via Business Today); OpenAI models on Google Cloud in private preview from 21 October; AEP's 702 MW, $4bn Bloom fuel-cell plant near Cheyenne under a 20-year PPA (15 October).

Sentiment cooled into the print: the stock fell 7.2% between 15 and 22 October amid a broader AI sell-off, and press reports record-wide CDS for Amazon, Alphabet and Meta in mid-October (no Alphabet level quoted).
checks: No subagent was used, so I verified the figures myself. Report date: confirmed on abc.xyz ('Alphabet Announces Date of Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Conference Call', 6 October 2026: Wednesday 28 October, 1:30 pm PT / 4:30 pm ET). MarketBeat still says 'not confirmed', which is out of date. Filing figures: I downloaded from EDGAR the 2Q26 8-K Ex. 99.1 (22 July 2026), the 2Q26 10-Q (23 July 2026), the 3Q25 Ex. 99.1 (29 October 2025), the 6 August 2026 FWP pricing term sheet and the 10 August 2026 8-K. I converted them to text and string-matched 52 figures in code: revenue, Cloud revenue and operating income, operating income, OCF, capex, FCF, TTM FCF, cash, debt, equity and notes proceeds, RPO, Cloud backlog, leases not yet commenced, the short-term lease, purchase commitments, backstops, credit-derivative notionals, the $24.1bn future backstops, the $20.0bn equity derivative, credit facilities, commercial paper, debt face value, TPU recognition timing, the August tranche sizes, spreads and ratings, and the 3Q25 comparatives. All matched. Call quotes (capex guide, 2027 'increase significantly', the bridging strategy, modest margin pressure, TPU timing, no further equity raises) come from the Benzinga transcript; the guide and backlog were cross-checked against MarketBeat's call highlights and OANDA. Consensus: I reopened the Zacks/Yahoo key-metrics article (EPS $2.94, revenue $111.64bn, Cloud $29.16bn, TAC $16.53bn), the Proactive/Yahoo BofA note (all six figures) and OANDA (all five figures), and each matched. Yahoo's analysis page, StockAnalysis's forecast and price history, MarketBeat, Pepperstone, Drillr, Admiral Markets, InsiderFinance and Top1Markets were each read once. Derived numbers were recomputed in Python: second-half capex needed ($114.4bn to $124.4bn), the 2Q Cloud margin of 35.6%, Cloud growth implied by Zacks (92.4%) and by BofA's 89%/93% ($28.6bn/$29.3bn), revenue growth of 24.9%, the ex-TAC reconciliation, EPS growth of 4.5%, the backstop totals ($51.4bn; $75.5bn including the $24.1bn), debt face of about $126bn after August, market cap of about $3.97tn, price moves, the SpaceX total ($29.4bn), backlog at 5.2x annualized Cloud revenue, the August tranche sum ($25.0bn), and Cipher's backstop (about $1.73bn). Inference: that the $111bn revenue consensus is net of TAC is our arithmetic; neither source says so. Single source or not primary: SpaceX contract terms (Euronews, citing SpaceX's IPO filing); Anthropic 3.5 GW (Business Today, citing a Broadcom filing); Meta TPU rental (SiliconANGLE, citing The Information); the Anthropic link to the private holding and the $20bn commitment (AI Weekly, citing Bloomberg; the 10-Q does not name it); 2027 capex of about $330bn (Wolfe via Invezz/Admiral) and about $300bn (BofA); FY27 FCF consensus (-$37bn Barchart; -$32bn TIKR); JPMorgan's 'approximately double' (Barron's via OANDA); Pichai's revenue-forgone comment (Barchart/Yahoo summary of a podcast). Fluidstack backstop sizes come from 2025 DCD reports and are not reconciled to the 10-Q notional. No Alphabet CDS level and no secondary bond spread was found for 22 or 23 October. The 23 October price is intraday. FY26 EPS consensus is not comparable across providers ($20.60 Yahoo, including equity gains; $13.14 StockAnalysis; $10.91 MarketBeat). No 3Q26 results had been filed when this card was built (latest EDGAR filing checked: 15 October 2026), and no post-results material was read.
consensus_thesis: Investors own Alphabet as the only hyperscaler with its own full stack (TPUs, Gemini, Cloud), and at about $3.97tn and about 24.6x forward earnings (Pepperstone) they are paying for Cloud growing near 90% off a $514bn backlog, with TPUs becoming a second, external revenue stream in 2027 that justifies roughly $200bn of 2026 capex and about $300bn or more in 2027. Positioning is crowded long (16 Buy, 1 Hold, 0 Sell per Pepperstone; average target about $430) but has cooled 7% into the print. In credit, Aa2/AA+ paper still clears at T+33 to T+130 bps, but hyperscaler CDS has widened to record levels as Alphabet funds the build with debt, equity and $43.8bn of off-balance-sheet backstops.
headline: 3Q26 will be judged less on another beat than on whether Google Cloud's near-90% growth and $514bn backlog can carry a capex bill heading for about $300bn in 2027, now that free cash flow is negative and Alphabet is backstopping tens of billions of third-party data center leases.
kona: Google has become the tenant-credit provider of last resort for AI data centers. It backstops neocloud leases as credit derivatives ($43.8bn notional at 30 June, with an estimated $24.1bn more agreed in principle), and keeps the right to take over the lease or pay a termination fee. At TeraWulf and Cipher those backstops ran to about $1.3bn to $1.7bn per site of 168 MW or more, alongside equity warrants. For Kona, that is the clearest route to investment-grade cash flows at a small off-grid site: host a Google-approved tenant (a Fluidstack-type neocloud serving a TPU or Anthropic-class buyer) on a long lease. The bar, though, is energized, grid-independent power, and so far the template has been used only on US sites of 100 MW or more. Kona's tens of MW in Argentina need to show either that Google will backstop at smaller scale abroad, or that its inference demand (Gemini at 22 billion API tokens a minute, Cloud capacity being rationed) leaves room for overflow capacity bought on shorter contracts.

name: Alphabet

questions.question: Your 10-Q shows credit-derivative backstops of third-party data center payments rising from $16.9bn at year-end to $43.8bn at 30 June, plus an agreement for an estimated $24.1bn more, on top of $7.6bn of energy guarantees. You say you can take over the leases on default. What was the notional at 30 September, how many counterparties and MW does it cover, and what share sits with Fluidstack or other unrated neoclouds? Will these backstops count against your own credit metrics in your planning, yes or no? If a counterparty defaults, would the resulting lease run through capex or opex?
questions.why: Backstops have become a second balance sheet that supports the neocloud build-out. They grew 2.6x in six months and are not in reported debt, so their size and concentration decide how much tail risk sits behind Aa2/AA+ paper, and how widely Google's credit reaches across the sector.

questions.question: In July you said free cash flow 'will remain under pressure', that operating cash flow funds first and debt second, and that you plan no more equity raises beyond the ATM. 2Q free cash flow was -$5.9bn, the Street models FY27 free cash flow near -$32bn to -$37bn, and since June you have raised $49.6bn of equity and more than $45bn of notes. What free cash flow do you expect for the second half of 2026? What range of debt issuance is in your 2027 plan? Will you commit to keeping the current ratings, and is there a net leverage ceiling?
questions.why: The investment case now rests on an external funding mix as well as on cash generation. A stated leverage ceiling or issuance range sets the supply overhang for hyperscaler bonds and the risk of further dilution.

questions.question: You have $85.2bn of leases not yet commenced, running to 2031, plus a $5.8bn short-term lease starting in 3Q, and press reports describe a SpaceX GPU contract at $920mn a month for 32 months. You also guided to 'modest margin pressure' in Cloud from third-party capacity. How much third-party capacity cost hit Cloud in 3Q, and how many MW or GPUs does it cover? How much of the $85.2bn commences in 2027? When do you expect owned capacity to replace rented capacity, by quarter?
questions.why: Rented capacity is a fixed cost carried on contracts, not capex. If it remains a lasting part of supply rather than a bridge, Cloud margins and lease-adjusted leverage both reset.

questions.question: You said capex will 'increase significantly in 2027'. The Street ranges from about $300bn (BofA) to about $330bn (Wolfe), against FY26 guidance of $195bn to $205bn. What is the 2027 framework? What share is servers against data centers and power? How much of it goes to TPUs for external customers, such as Anthropic's 3.5 GW from 2027, compared with internal training?
questions.why: The 2027 capex number is the single largest driver of the stock's free cash flow case. The split between servers and buildings, and between external and internal use, tells whether spend is matched to contracted revenue.

questions.question: Cloud backlog reached $514bn, just over half to be recognized within 24 months, and it now includes TPU system sales. What was backlog at 30 September? How much of the change came from Anthropic, Meta or other TPU commitments? What TPU system revenue was in 3Q, and what do you expect in 2027? Pichai said last week that Cloud is giving up revenue so research gets compute. Can you size the demand you turned away in 3Q?
questions.why: TPU sales are the bull case for 2027 (BofA calls it the 'key 2027 upside case'). Concentration in one or two AI labs turns a $514bn backlog into counterparty exposure, and Anthropic's capacity is conditional on its 'continued commercial success' (Broadcom).

questions.question: You have energy take-or-pay contracts out to 2054, $7.6bn of guarantees for counterparties' power equipment, and AEP's 702 MW Bloom fuel-cell plant near Cheyenne under a 20-year PPA from 2028. What share of capacity coming online in 2027 and 2028 is behind-the-meter or on-site generation rather than grid supply? Are the $7.6bn of guarantees that expired in September being renewed or turned into PPAs?
questions.why: Power is the binding constraint on capacity. Guarantees and take-or-pay contracts add commitments of a debt-like kind, and how much Google relies on behind-the-meter generation shows whether off-grid sites can compete for its demand.

risks: Cloud deceleration or margin compression as rented third-party capacity (including SpaceX GPUs) and depreciation grow faster than revenue.
The capex trajectory (about $200bn in 2026, about $300bn to $330bn in 2027 on Street views) keeps free cash flow negative and requires steady debt and equity issuance.
Off-balance-sheet exposure: $43.8bn of credit-derivative backstops to third-party data centers, $85.2bn of leases not yet commenced, and $811.0bn of purchase commitments.
Concentration of TPU and backlog demand in a few AI labs (Anthropic, Meta), with Anthropic's capacity described as dependent on its commercial success.
Earnings quality and macro: EPS swings from mark-to-market on SpaceX and private stakes, Search disruption from AI assistants, DOJ and EU remedies, and the Fed decision on the same day (28 October).

sections.body: For AI compute, Alphabet is a buyer and financier. It builds and leases data centers for its own TPUs and GPUs, sells that capacity as Google Cloud (GCP consumption, AI infrastructure, and since 2Q26 TPU systems installed in customer data centers), and serves Gemini and Search internally. Compute goes first to frontier research (DeepMind), then to Google's own products and Cloud. When in-house supply falls short, Alphabet rents third-party capacity (neoclouds, SpaceX) and backstops lease payments of third-party data center developers, booked as credit derivatives. That capacity is funded by about $185.7bn of TTM operating cash flow, $242.5bn of cash and securities, Aa2/AA+ senior notes, a June equity raise, and long-term supply and energy take-or-pay contracts.
